html:
The Glagolitic script is the oldest known Slavic alphabet, created in the 860s by the Byzantine monk Constantine, later called Cyril. He made it for the mission he and his brother Methodius led to Great Moravia, so that the gospels and church services could be put into Old Church Slavonic.

Its letters were new shapes, not a copy of any one alphabet, though scholars see hints of Greek handwriting and other scripts. It had about forty letters to fit the sounds of Slavic speech.

After Methodius died in 885 his followers were driven out of Moravia and went to the First Bulgarian Empire. There Glagolitic was used at Ohrid, while at Preslav scholars built the simpler Cyrillic script from Greek letters, and Cyrillic soon won out. Glagolitic lasted longest in Croatia, where priests on the Adriatic coast used it in the Latin Mass into modern times. The Baška tablet of about 1100, a key early Croatian text, is carved in Glagolitic.
